prompt: A company rewards its best senior engineer by naming her architect, calling it "the next rung". Which idea from lesson 16 does that framing miss?

choices.text: That architects are paid less than senior engineers
choices.why: Pay is not what the lesson discusses.

choices.text: That the new job is a different scope and horizon, not more of the old one
choices.why: Right: changing role swaps one box for another, and some of what made her good will not help.

choices.text: That architects stop writing code once named
choices.why: Lesson 15 argues the opposite.

choices.text: That the title has to come with a team to manage
choices.why: The architect manages nobody, by lesson 16's last section.

prompt: A staff engineer spends a year running the CTO's reorganisation of three departments, deciding in her name. Which of Larson's archetypes fits?

choices.text: Solver
choices.why: A solver goes deep into hard technical problems; this is acting for an executive.

choices.text: Architect
choices.why: The architect answers for an area of the system over time, with authority of their own.

choices.text: Tech lead of the three departments
choices.why: A tech lead guides one team's approach and execution.

choices.text: Right hand
choices.why: Right: she extends the CTO's reach with his scope and authority.

prompt: Under Carreto's decision-rights table, Matching wants to keep a copy of the drivers' bank details that Payments holds. Who decides?

choices.text: Matching's tech lead, since the copy would live in Matching's database
choices.why: Where the copy lives does not change whose data it is.

choices.text: Payments' tech lead, as the owner of the original
choices.why: He must be asked; the table gives data ownership to the architect.

choices.text: The architect, after asking both tech leads
choices.why: Right: who owns which data and who may read it is one of her two rows.

choices.text: Platform, because a copy needs replication
choices.why: Platform may be asked about the mechanism; the ownership question is not theirs.

prompt: An architect proposes to review every pull request: 300 a week at 9 minutes each. How many hours a week is that?
hint: Lesson 16. Minutes in total, divided by 60.

prompt: Which of these lie outside the architect's role, by lesson 16? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Deciding which feature the Shipper team builds next
choices.why: Yes: product priorities are Helena's.

choices.text: Holding the ticket a team's release depends on
choices.why: Yes: the architect stays off the critical path.

choices.text: Deciding whether a new database goes into production
choices.why: That row is the architect's.

choices.text: Choosing who is promoted on the Tracking team
choices.why: Yes: promotions belong to the engineering manager.

choices.text: Keeping the standards and their automated checks
choices.why: Standards and their enforcement stay inside the boundary (lesson 9).

prompt: Which question is the tech lead the one person on a team to answer, by lesson 16?

choices.text: How does this team build what it has to build?
choices.why: Right: the team's internal design and the way it works on the code.

choices.text: What does the company build next year?
choices.why: That is product's, at company scope.

choices.text: Who owns the data that is shared between several teams?
choices.why: Data ownership across teams is the architect's row.

choices.text: Who on the team gets a raise this year?
choices.why: Pay and promotion are the engineering manager's.
